name: Brent Mason
notes: The defining Nashville lead-guitar grammar, placed in PRODUCERS by the research as an *instrumental-grammar* entry — "the Nashville lead-guitar, pedal-steel and drum vocabularies that the engine needs as style parameters; no artist entry duplicates them" (Assignment notes). ⛔ **This file exists because that instruction says it should.** It was dropped in the first encoding pass under a "Drums: n/a" gate, which reads the wrong field: the entry's Drums line is not empty, it is a *placement* rule for his own part, and this entry carries more documented technique than the two drummer entries that were shipped. The lick vocabulary is the model: "double-stops in sixths and thirds, open-string pull-offs, chromatic approach notes into chord tones, and pedal-steel-imitating bends against a held note" — so `intervals.third` is the highest in this section and the sixths read as the leap share, `halfStepDissonance` is 0.16 against the genre's 0.02 (that is the chromatic approach, and nothing else in country-pop authors one), and `chordToneBias` stays high because those approaches resolve *into chord tones*. `articulation` is the entry's own word: "staccato 'chicken-pickin'' attacks land on the backbeat and the 16ths around it, and he leaves the downbeat to the band" — hence the 16th-level density and no drum block at all, because the downbeat belongs to the band. The phrase grid is quoted: fills "answer the vocal in the gaps at the ends of **2- and 4-bar phrases**," which is `phraseBars` and the counter's `fillGapsOnly`. The bass block follows the one low-register fact the entry gives — "a Jerry Jones six-string bass tuned down an octave and a Jerry Jones baritone tuned down a fourth are documented parts of his kit, i.e. the 'tic-tac' baritone doubling of the bass line is in-palette" — so the line is root-following rather than independent, because a tic-tac double *is* the bass line. The arrangement carries his stated method: "not playing the obvious … he works inside each artist's framework rather than deploying signature licks uniformly," which is a high `switchUpProb` (he does not repeat himself across songs), and "on artists who wanted dance-length breaks he supplied **extended instrumental passages** rather than short solos," which is the 8-bar bridge — ⚠ the engine's section vocabulary is intro / verse / prechorus / chorus / bridge / outro and has no instrumental kind, so the documented instrumental break is carried by the bridge's length. ⚠ **No `session.bpm` and no `session.keys` are authored, and both omissions are the research's own words**: "his parts run across the whole tempo map at 2&4" (so the genre band stands) and "he plays in the singer's key, not the guitarist's, which is precisely why the lick vocabulary is transposition-robust" (so no key set is claimed). ⚠ **No `chords` block is authored**: the entry contains no roman numerals and no harmonic statement at all, so the genre's families are inherited rather than invented — the same call `dann-huff`, `byron-gallimore`, `nathan-chapman` and `ed-seay` already ship. ⚠ The humanize values are read from "light 9–44 strings with normal action for **fast session work**" and the same interview's "first takes usually kept" (quoted in this document's `country-train` timbre palette), i.e. a played, uncorrected feel — but the numbers themselves are INFERRED, and no per-lane `timingJitterMs` is authored because the entry's Drums line is about *his* placement, not about a kit he plays. ⚠ Also INFERRED: the melody register, the density range, the contour split, the counter ratio and every bass number except the root-following rationale. ⚠ Confidence is medium (research: high) — the technique is first-person and detailed, but this entry supplies no tempo, no key and no numeral, so most of what a generator needs here is this author's reading rather than a researched fact. ⚠ `relatedGenres` claims `country-train` on the document's own words and nothing wider: that section's timbre palette is sourced to this same interview — "the Nashville session-Telecaster tone that carries this archetype on record is documented concretely: a 1968 Telecaster … into a **Boss compressor** into a **1967 Fender Deluxe Reverb** … ([Premier Guitar — Brent Mason interview])" — and the Assignment notes flag the fast Alan Jackson and Brooks & Dunn grooves ("Chattahoochee," "Mercury Blues," "Boot Scootin' Boogie"), records this entry's own credit list names him on, to `country-train`.
